opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core intuition is that the naive way of steering, where you find a direction for a concept and just add some multiple of that vector to the activations, assumes the concept lives on a straight line. When you actually look at how models represent things, that's often not true. Concepts tend to live on curved, lower-dimensional structures inside activation space. Days of the week or months of the year sit on something like a circle. Other concepts have more complicated geometry, but the point is they're not linear rays shooting off to infinity.

So if you take a linear step, even a well-chosen one, you move off the region where the model's real activations live. A small push might be fine, but as you push harder you end up in activation space the model has never seen during training. That's where you get the familiar failure modes: the model gets incoherent, starts repeating itself, loses fluency, or the steering just stops doing what you wanted because the downstream layers don't know how to interpret that point.

If instead you move along the manifold, tracing the path that real activations actually take as the concept varies, you stay in-distribution. Every intermediate point looks like something the model could naturally produce, so the later layers read it the way they normally would. You get a smoother, more controllable change in behavior and you can push further before things break.

There's also an interpretability angle I find exciting. If following the manifold steers better than a straight line, that tells you something about how the model organizes knowledge. Steering becomes a test of whether you've found the right geometry. When the curved path works and the linear one doesn't, that's evidence the model is doing something richer than the linear representation hypothesis on its own would suggest.

So the short version is that the model has its own map of the concept, and steering works better when you follow that map instead of cutting a straight line through territory the model doesn't recognize.

r001.rationale: It says a linear steering step can leave the region of activations seen during training, especially as the push grows.

r002.rationale: It describes following the path real activations take as the concept varies, with meaningful intermediate points and a smoother change in behavior.

r003.rationale: It attributes linear steering’s limited range and resulting failures to moving off the concept’s curved activation structure.

r004.rationale: It says manifold steering supports a smoother, more controllable behavior change while keeping intermediate activations in-distribution and letting later layers interpret them normally.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that a concept inside a model isn't a single point or a single direction, it's a shape. If you look at how a model represents something like "sadness" or "formality" or "the user is asking a coding question," the activations that encode it don't sit on one line through the residual stream. They form a curved, lower-dimensional surface, a manifold, and where you are on that surface carries meaning. Intensity, context, how the concept interacts with everything else the model is tracking at that moment.

The classic steering approach ignores that. You take a mean difference vector, you add some scaled version of it, and you push the activations in a straight line. For small nudges that works fine, because locally the manifold looks flat. But the moment you push harder, you walk straight off the surface into a region the model has never actually occupied during training. And that's where you get the familiar failure modes: the model starts repeating itself, the grammar degrades, it says "love love love" or produces text that's technically on-topic but weirdly broken. You've put it in an out-of-distribution state and it doesn't know how to behave there.

Following the manifold means instead of moving in a straight line, you move along the surface. You ask, from where the model currently is, what's the nearby state that has more of this concept and is still a state the model would naturally produce? Then you take that step, re-evaluate, and step again. You're tracing a path through the model's own representational geometry rather than imposing one from outside.

What you get from that is two things. First, you can steer much more strongly before coherence collapses, because every intermediate point is a plausible internal state. Second, and I think this is the underappreciated part, the steering is more faithful to what the concept actually is. A straight vector for "happiness" tends to drag along whatever happened to correlate with happiness in your contrast set. Moving along the manifold stays inside the structure the model learned, so the side effects are smaller and the behavior change is more specific.

I'd also say it reframes how we should think about interpretability more generally. If concepts are manifolds, then a lot of the tools we've been using, linear probes, single directions, are approximations that work in a neighborhood and quietly fail outside it. Steering is just the place where that failure becomes very visible very quickly.

r001.rationale: It says straight-line steering can push activations off the manifold into states the model never occupied during training, causing out-of-distribution failures.

r002.rationale: It describes taking repeated steps along the manifold toward states with more of the concept, tracing a path through the model’s representational geometry.

r003.rationale: It explains that linear steering works for small nudges but fails at larger ones because it ignores the manifold and pushes representations off its surface.

r004.rationale: It says manifold-following allows stronger steering before coherence collapses and keeps intermediate states plausible, while making behavior changes more specific with smaller side effects.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that a concept isn’t necessarily represented as a single direction that means the same thing everywhere in a model’s activation space. How it’s represented can depend on the context. So if you find a vector and push along it, that might work locally, but as you push farther, you can start changing things you didn’t intend to change.

Following the concept’s manifold means accounting for that geometry. You adjust the direction as you move, so you’re trying to stay in regions that correspond to coherent expressions of the concept. Ideally, that gives you more control over the property you care about while preserving the rest of the model’s behavior.

Of course, that depends on how well you’ve actually identified the manifold. But the basic intuition is that steering should follow the structure of the representation, rather than assume that structure is linear.

r001.rationale: It says a fixed vector can cause unintended changes as it moves farther, but does not explain that linear steering can pass through representations outside the model’s distribution.

r002.rationale: It describes staying in regions with coherent expressions of the concept, but does not state that this enables smooth interpolation between meaningful concept values.

r003.rationale: It notes that a fixed direction may work locally, but does not attribute earlier steering’s narrow effective range to failing to respect the concept manifold’s geometry.

r004.rationale: It says manifold-based steering offers more control over the property while preserving the rest of the model’s behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intuition is that a concept isn’t necessarily represented as one fixed direction in a model’s activation space. Its representation depends on context. So if you take a single vector and push in that direction everywhere, it might work in some settings, but in others you’re pushing the model somewhere that doesn’t correspond to the concept you intended.

Following the manifold means trying to respect that local structure. You’re asking, “Given where the model is right now, what change would move it toward this concept?” That direction can change as the context changes.

The hope is that you get more consistent steering with fewer unintended effects, because you’re working with the model’s learned representations. The challenge, of course, is identifying that structure accurately enough that following it actually helps.

r001.rationale: It says a fixed vector may not match the intended concept in some contexts, but does not state that linear steering across a curved manifold can pass through representations outside the model's distribution.

r002.rationale: It describes context-dependent steering directions, but does not say manifold following enables smooth interpolation between meaningful concept values.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss earlier feature steering or attribute its narrow effective range to ignoring manifold geometry.

r004.rationale: It hopes for fewer unintended effects, but does not state that manifold steering can change a represented characteristic without degrading the model's output.
